title: NURS 1017 Unit 3 Case Study 6
description: 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease (HbSS) in a vaso-occlusive crisis with fever; carrier parents and a family history of Huntington disease and hemophilia B, comparing autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant and X-linked recessive inheritance.

authorReview.note: Revised by Claude on 24 Nov 2026 from the author's draft (New Case Study 2). leftContent.intro: The nurse in the pediatric emergency department is assessing Marcus, a 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease (HbSS), brought in by his parents for severe leg and lower-back pain.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.content:
1400:Marcus (diagnosed with sickle cell disease on newborn screening) arrives with his mother and father. Runny nose and mild cough for 2 days; has been drinking very little. Over the past 12 hours, worsening deep, throbbing pain in both thighs, knees and lower back; rates pain 8/10 on the FACES scale and refuses to walk. Irritable, guarding both legs. Mild scleral icterus and pale conjunctivae, which his mother says are “how his eyes usually look.” Oral mucous membranes dry; capillary refill 3 seconds. Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally; no chest pain. Abdomen soft and non-tender; spleen not palpable. No focal neurologic deficits.

1415:Family history: both parents are healthy and have sickle cell trait (HbAS). Marcus's mother says her 44-year-old brother was recently diagnosed with Huntington disease and asks whether Marcus could get it too. Marcus's father says his sister's 9-year-old son has hemophilia B. Pediatrician and hematology notified.

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Thigh, knee and lower-back pain rated 8/10, refusing to walk
Heart rate 134 beats/min
Lungs clear to auscultation with no chest pain
SpO₂ 93% on room air with RR 26 breaths/min
Spleen not palpable
Dry oral mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, and little fluid intake for 2 days
Temperature 38.3° C
BP 102/62 mm Hg with no focal neurologic deficits

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: deep bone and joint pain that stops a child walking is the hallmark of a vaso-occlusive crisis: sickled red cells block small vessels and the tissue becomes ischemic (Option 1). A temperature of 38.3° C is urgent in sickle cell disease: repeated splenic infarcts leave the spleen unable to clear encapsulated bacteria (functional asplenia), so fever can mean life-threatening bacteremia (Option 7). Low SpO₂ with a fast RR increases sickling and can be the start of acute chest syndrome (Option 4). Tachycardia reflects pain, fever, dehydration and anemia (Option 2). Dehydration raises blood viscosity and, with the viral illness, likely triggered this crisis (Option 6).

Do not require follow-up now: clear lungs without chest pain make acute chest syndrome less likely at this moment, though it can develop later (Option 3). By school age, most children with HbSS have a small, scarred spleen that cannot be felt; a newly enlarged spleen would suggest splenic sequestration (Option 5). Normal BP and no focal deficits are reassuring; a sudden deficit would suggest a stroke (Option 8). The mild icterus and pallor are his usual signs of chronic hemolysis; his hemoglobin will be compared with his baseline.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is consistent with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked recessive inheritance.

rows.text: Marcus has sickle cell disease although both of his parents are healthy
Marcus's maternal grandmother and her son both developed a movement disorder in adulthood
Marcus's father's sister is healthy, but her son has hemophilia B
Each of Marcus's parents has one HbS allele and no symptoms
Symptoms may not begin until mid-adulthood, often after the person has had children
The disorder occurs almost only in males, who inherit the gene from their mothers

question.explanation:
Autosomal recessive (sickle cell disease): disease appears only with two mutated alleles (homozygous HbSS). Carriers (heterozygous HbAS) are healthy, so an affected child often has two unaffected parents. Marcus's results show active hemolysis: hemoglobin below his usual level, high reticulocytes (the marrow compensating) and high indirect bilirubin. Howell-Jolly bodies on the smear mean the spleen no longer filters the blood.

Autosomal dominant (Huntington disease): one mutated allele causes the disease, so it appears in every generation (grandmother, then her son) and affects males and females alike. Because symptoms usually start between 30 and 50, people often have children before they know they carry it. Marcus's mother has a 50% chance of carrying the gene, so Marcus's own risk is 25% at present; predictive testing of children is not recommended and is left for him to decide as an adult.

X-linked recessive (hemophilia B): the gene is on the X chromosome. Males have one X, so one mutated copy causes disease; females with one normal X are usually healthy carriers who pass it to half their sons. The paternal aunt is a carrier. Marcus's father is an unaffected male, so he does not carry the gene and cannot pass it to Marcus.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1600 and the Vital Signs.
question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: Sickle cell disease is caused by a [[drop0]] in the beta-globin (HBB) gene. Given Marcus's temperature, SpO₂ and respiratory rate, the nurse's priority is to prevent [[drop1]]. Because both parents are carriers (HbAS), each future pregnancy has a [[drop2]] chance of a child with sickle cell disease.

options.text: trinucleotide repeat expansion
nondisjunction of chromosome 11
point mutation (one base substituted)
teratogenic exposure before birth
splenic sequestration crisis
acute kidney injury from dehydration
acute chest syndrome and sepsis
ischemic stroke

question.explanation:
Point mutation: a single base change in HBB puts valine in place of glutamic acid in beta-globin, creating the HbS allele. A trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion causes Huntington disease; nondisjunction causes aneuploidy such as Down syndrome; a teratogen damages development without changing the genes.

Priority: fever of 38.6° C in a child without a working spleen can progress to overwhelming sepsis within hours, and falling SpO₂ (92%) with a rising RR (28 breaths/min) increases sickling in the lungs, the path to acute chest syndrome, the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease. A non-palpable spleen and normal neurologic findings do not point to sequestration or stroke now; dehydration is being treated with IV fluids.

25%: HbAS × HbAS gives, with each pregnancy, 25% HbAA (unaffected, not a carrier), 50% HbAS (carrier) and 25% HbSS (affected). 50% is the chance of a carrier child, 75% the chance of an unaffected child, and 2 in 3 the chance that an unaffected sibling is a carrier.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1630 and the Orders.
question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in Marcus's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give the scheduled morphine and ketorolac and reassess pain with the FACES scale
Cover Marcus with a warm blanket and keep the room comfortably warm
Apply ice packs to the painful knees and lower back for 20 minutes every hour
Request IV fluid boluses at twice the maintenance rate to flush out the sickled cells
Give the first dose of ceftriaxone without delay now that blood cultures are drawn
Run the IV fluids at the ordered rate and offer oral fluids often
Give oxygen to keep SpO₂ at 95% or higher and coach incentive spirometry every 2 hours while awake

question.explanation:
Include: hydration lowers blood viscosity and slows sickling (Option 6). Vaso-occlusive pain is severe ischemic pain; scheduled opioid plus NSAID with regular reassessment controls it better than waiting for the child to ask (Option 1). Oxygen corrects hypoxemia, and incentive spirometry prevents the atelectasis that leads to acute chest syndrome, especially when opioids and splinting make breathing shallow (Option 7). With functional asplenia, a febrile child receives IV antibiotics promptly once cultures are drawn (Option 5). Warmth dilates vessels and eases pain (Option 2).

Do not include: cold causes vasoconstriction, which slows blood flow and worsens sickling (Option 3). Fluids are given at about 1 to 1.5 times maintenance once dehydration is corrected; overhydration can cause pulmonary edema and trigger acute chest syndrome (Option 4).

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Request IV meperidine for breakthrough pain
Monitor for new chest pain, cough, fast breathing or falling SpO₂
Request a repeat hemoglobin electrophoresis each morning
Check the spleen size and watch for sudden pallor or a drop in hemoglobin
Place ice packs on the thighs and lower back between morphine doses
Assess respiratory rate and sedation level before and after each morphine dose

question.explanation:
Meperidine (Contraindicated): its metabolite normeperidine accumulates with repeated doses and lowers the seizure threshold; it is not used for sickle cell pain.

Watch for acute chest syndrome (Indicated): it often develops 24 to 72 hours into an admission for a pain crisis: new chest pain, cough, fever, tachypnea, falling SpO₂ and a new infiltrate on X-ray.

Daily electrophoresis (Non-Essential): his HbSS genotype does not change; the daily CBC and reticulocyte count track the anemia.

Spleen and pallor (Indicated): splenic sequestration (sudden spleen enlargement trapping blood) and aplastic crisis (often after parvovirus B19) both cause a rapid fall in hemoglobin and need emergency care.

Ice packs (Contraindicated): cold causes vasoconstriction and more sickling.

Respiratory rate and sedation (Indicated): opioid-induced hypoventilation would worsen hypoxemia and sickling; increasing sedation comes before respiratory depression.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The parents show understanding when they say they will bring Marcus to the emergency department for [[drop0]]. They understand that hydroxyurea prevents crises by [[drop1]]. Marcus's mother understands that if she carries the Huntington disease gene, each of her children has [[drop2]] of inheriting it.

question.explanation:
When to come to the emergency department: fever of 38.5° C or higher (sepsis risk without a working spleen), chest pain, cough or fast breathing (acute chest syndrome), sudden pallor, weakness or an enlarging abdomen (splenic sequestration or aplastic crisis), any neurologic change (stroke), priapism, or pain not relieved at home. Mild pain that settles with home measures, a cold without fever, and his usual mild icterus can be managed at home.

Hydroxyurea: it raises fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which does not polymerize and dilutes HbS inside the red cell, so cells sickle less; crises, acute chest syndrome and transfusions become less frequent. It does not change his genes. It can lower blood counts, so CBCs are monitored.

Autosomal dominant inheritance: one mutated allele is enough, so a parent who carries the gene passes it to each child with a 50% chance, regardless of sex. Carriers develop symptoms later in life, so not yet having symptoms does not rule it out. 25% applies to two carriers of a recessive condition; sex-limited risk applies to X-linked conditions.
